```{r knitr_init, echo=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
options(max.print=200)
opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE, comment=NA, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
```

# Preparation: load and clean the data

This is exactly the cleaning from the exercise sheet. Run it first, so that `dat` is ready for the exercises.

```{r}
dat <- read.delim('https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/zqjdoi7naolmruyxrraxq/diabetes_2025.tsv?rlkey=txnps3ccr0vj47yvjmpecbeom&dl=1')

dat <- select(dat, -bp.2s, -bp.2d, -time.ppn)
dat <- select(dat, gender, location, frame, age, height, weight, waist, hip,
              stab.glu, glyhb, chol, hdl, ratio, bp.1s, bp.1d)
dat <- drop_na(dat)
```

# Exercise 1: Data Exploration and Summary Statistics

### 1.1 Mean and standard deviation of hdl

```{r}
mean(dat$hdl)
sd(dat$hdl)
```

### 1.2 Body Mass Index

`mutate()` adds a new column. Inside `mutate()` we can use the column names directly.

```{r}
dat <- mutate(dat, bmi = weight / height^2 * 703)
head(dat$bmi)
```

### 1.3 Patients per location

```{r}
table(dat$location)
```

The location with the most patients is the one with the largest number in the table. R can also tell us its name:

```{r}
names(which.max(table(dat$location)))
```

### 1.4 Median age of men and women

```{r}
men   <- filter(dat, gender == "male")
women <- filter(dat, gender == "female")

median(men$age)
median(women$age)
```

Compare the two numbers: if they differ by only a few years, the two groups are similar in age.

# Exercise 2: Visualizing Relationships Between Variables

### 2.1 Scatter plot weight vs height

```{r}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = height, y = weight)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)
```

Taller people tend to be heavier: the points go from bottom left to top right, so there is a (positive) relationship. It is not perfect, because people of the same height can have very different weights.

### 2.2 Color by gender

```{r}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = height, y = weight, color = gender)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)
```

Check whether one gender is shifted to the upper right (typically men are taller and heavier than women), and whether the relationship itself (taller = heavier) looks similar in both groups.

### 2.3 Correlation

```{r}
cor(dat$weight, dat$height)
```

The correlation coefficient is between -1 and 1. A value close to 0 means no linear relationship, a value close to 1 means a strong positive relationship. Read off the value above to judge how strong the relationship is.

### 2.4 Boxplots of cholesterol by gender

```{r}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = gender, y = chol)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

Compare the thick middle lines (medians) and the heights of the boxes. Other variables work in the same way, you only change `y`:

```{r}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = gender, y = hdl)) +
  geom_boxplot()

ggplot(dat, aes(x = gender, y = weight)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

# Going further: Advanced Data Manipulation

### 1. Age groups

`cut()` splits numbers into intervals. With `right = FALSE`, each interval includes its left border: 40 belongs to "middle", and 60 belongs to "senior".

```{r}
dat <- mutate(dat, age_group = cut(age,
                                   breaks = c(-Inf, 40, 60, Inf),
                                   labels = c("young", "middle", "senior"),
                                   right = FALSE))
table(dat$age_group)
```

### 2. Mean cholesterol per gender and age group

The symbol `%>%` ("pipe") means "take the result on the left and give it to the function on the right".

```{r}
chol.means <- dat %>%
  group_by(gender, age_group) %>%
  summarise(mean_chol = mean(chol))

chol.means
```

### 3. Standardize function

```{r}
standardize <- function(x) {
  (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
}

# Test: the result should have mean 0 and standard deviation 1
mean(standardize(dat$age))
sd(standardize(dat$age))
```

Now we apply it only to the numeric columns. First we find which columns are numeric:

```{r}
is.num <- sapply(dat, is.numeric)
is.num
```

```{r}
dat.scaled <- dat
dat.scaled[, is.num] <- apply(dat[, is.num], MARGIN = 2, FUN = standardize)

head(dat.scaled)
```

The text columns (`gender`, `location`, `frame`) and `age_group` are not changed.

### 4. Most extreme BMI

A value far away from 0 is extreme. We use `abs()` so that both very high and very low values count, and `which.max()` to get the row number.

```{r}
row.extreme <- which.max(abs(dat.scaled$bmi))
row.extreme

# standardized BMI of this patient
dat.scaled$bmi[row.extreme]

# all clinical information (original values)
dat[row.extreme, ]
```

To see what is unusual, compare the values of this patient with the typical values in the dataset (`summary(dat)`): the BMI is many standard deviations away from the mean. Look at `weight` and `height` of this patient: BMI is high when the weight is large compared to the height (or low when it is very small).

```{r}
summary(dat$bmi)
```
